input.content:
You are building a frozen evidence-source packet for a focused PFAS treatment
review. Use Web Search to locate independent primary studies, pilot or field
deployments, or quantitative modeling/life-cycle studies that directly address
the task. The defining review is held out and is an exclusion target, not an
evidence source.

Search broadly and return every independently verified eligible primary source
found within the requested candidate-screening ceiling. There is no fixed final
source count and no penalty for retaining multiple eligible studies that address
similar evidence categories. Continue searching across distinct formulations
until the ceiling is reached or additional searches yield no new eligible
sources. Order retained sources from strongest and most complementary to
weakest. Favor sources that collectively cover all task components and preserve PFAS identity,
water matrix, concentration or loading, operating conditions, scale, endpoint,
quantitative result, limitations, residuals, energy, and cost where available.
Review articles and perspectives may help discovery but must not appear in the
  source packet.

For every retained source:

- provide the exact URL inspected by Web Search, matching the URL surfaced by
  the search tool rather than substituting a different repository or index;
- provide a DOI when one is stated by the inspected source;
- identify the publication year and publication status conservatively;
- identify the access scope conservatively;
- include only short evidence passages actually visible in the inspected
  source, each with a stable local locator_id;
- mark a passage verbatim only when it is copied exactly; otherwise mark it as
  a paraphrase;
- never turn a search-result snippet into study evidence; and
- leave unsupported fields empty rather than infer them.

Prefer peer-reviewed articles. Use a preprint, conference abstract, or report
only when it supplies distinct task-relevant evidence unavailable from a
peer-reviewed source, and label its status explicitly.

Do not cite, reconstruct, or use the held-out review. Source and locator IDs are
temporary capture identifiers and will be deterministically renumbered after
validation. Return one JSON object following the supplied schema exactly.

Focused review task:
{"review_brief":"Prepare a focused, data-grounded review explaining how an engineer should select an adsorption medium for a specified PFAS profile and water matrix.","task_id":"RT01","title":"Selecting an adsorption medium for a defined PFAS water-treatment application"}

Required components:
[{"component_id":"RT01-C1","requirement":"Compare the adsorption mechanisms and material properties most relevant to PFAS chain length, functional group, and precursor composition."},{"component_id":"RT01-C2","requirement":"Evaluate how dissolved organic matter, inorganic ions, pH, competing contaminants, and influent concentration alter performance."},{"component_id":"RT01-C3","requirement":"Translate the evidence into conditional media-selection criteria rather than a universal material ranking."}]

Task-specific extraction objective:
Extract adsorbent identity and properties, PFAS identity, water matrix, influent concentration, pH, co-constituents, dose or bed conditions, adsorption endpoint, quantitative result, and reported mechanism.

Held-out anchor identifiers:
{"all_blocked_dois":["10.1016/j.envpol.2023.121138"],"all_blocked_titles":["a review of pfas adsorption from aqueous solutions current approaches engineering applications challenges and opportunities"],"all_blocked_urls":["https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envpol.2023.121138"],"anchor_id":"AR-LEI-2023","corpus_source":"2023 - Lei - A review of PFAS adsorption from aqueous solutions - Current approaches, engineering applications, challenges, and opportunities.pdf","doi":"10.1016/j.envpol.2023.121138","title":"A review of PFAS adsorption from aqueous solutions: Current approaches, engineering applications, challenges, and opportunities","url":"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envpol.2023.121138"}

Maximum eligible primary sources to inspect and return:
20

Minimum retained sources required for a usable review packet:
6

Search for and inspect independent primary sources. Do not stop after reaching
the minimum. Return every eligible nonduplicate source found before the search
ceiling or evidence-search saturation, after checking the exclusion list and
source type.

search_notes: Web search was used to identify primary experimental and modeling studies on PFAS adsorption relevant to media selection across activated carbons, anion exchange resins, colloidal activated carbon, and emerging mineral adsorbents.

Several highly relevant ScienceDirect articles (e.g., on PFAS competitive adsorption to GAC and AER, and some classic PFOS/PFOA sorption studies) could not be accessed directly due to 403 restrictions; where alternative repositories (institutional servers, ResearchGate, KIT or SLU archives) provided full PDFs, those were used instead.

Regulatory and review documents (EPA technical support documents, Health Canada guidance, and narrative PFAS adsorption reviews) were used only for context and discovery and were not included as primary evidence sources, consistent with instructions.
Some recent and highly relevant activated carbon and ion-exchange studies hosted on PubMed Central were blocked by reCAPTCHA and therefore excluded from the packet despite strong topic alignment.

Within the 20-source ceiling, seven non-duplicate primary studies were retained that together cover PFAS structural effects on adsorption, water-matrix impacts (groundwater vs deionized water, inorganic anions, limited DOC), and conditional criteria for selecting adsorption media for defined PFAS profiles.

sources.citation: Riegel M, Haist-Gulde B, Sacher F. Sorptive removal of short-chain perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) during drinking water treatment using activated carbon and anion exchanger. Environmental Sciences Europe. 2023;35(1):12.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Methods/Results – Batch sorption (PDF p.4-5, Fig. 1, Table 5)
evidence_passages.passage: Batch isotherms for PFBA, PFPeA, PFHxA, PFHpA and PFOA were measured in demineralized water spiked at 6 µg/L per PFAS with pulverized GAC; Freundlich K_F increased with chain length.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Methods/Results – Ion exchange batch tests (PDF p.4-5, Fig. 2, Table 6)
evidence_passages.passage: Using tap water spiked with eight PFAS at 100 µg/L each and pH 7±0.3, Langmuir isotherms on strong-base anion exchanger K6362 showed the adsorption affinity order PFOS > PFHxS > PFBS ≈ PFOA > PFHpA > PFHxA > PFPeA > PFBA.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Results – Pilot-scale GAC column (PDF p.6, Fig. 5)
evidence_passages.passage: For contaminated groundwater in a pilot GAC column (GAC-CC, 1 m bed, 7.5 m/h), 10% breakthrough occurred at about 6,000 BV for PFBA, 11,000 BV for PFPeA, 16,000 BV for PFHxA, 20,000 BV for PFHpA and 23,000 BV for PFOA.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Results – Pilot-scale GAC column (PDF p.6, lines 533–540)
evidence_passages.passage: At 10% breakthrough in the pilot GAC column, calculated GAC loadings were roughly 2.4 µg/g (PFBA), 17 µg/g (PFPeA), 21 µg/g (PFHxA), 11 µg/g (PFHpA) and 29 µg/g (PFOA).

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Results – IEX pilot column (PDF p.7, Fig. 7)
evidence_passages.passage: Column tests with weak-base resin D5706 treating real PFAS‑contaminated groundwater (EBCT 2.4–6 min) showed 10% breakthrough of PFBA at ~4,000 BV, PFPeA at ~10,000 BV and PFHxA at ~25,000 BV.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Discussion – Selection of GAC (PDF p.6, lines 497–507, 508–516, 541–552)
evidence_passages.passage: The authors conclude that optimal GAC selection for PFAS removal depends strongly on PFAS chain-length distribution and target effluent levels; some carbons favored PFOA removal while others performed better for PFBA.

source_limitations: Groundwater matrix chemistry (e.g., detailed DOC, inorganic ion composition) is summarized in tables not fully captured here.
Study focuses mainly on PFCAs and one PFSA; many newer PFAS chemistries and precursors are not included.
Pilot columns are specific to one European groundwater and may not represent other waters with very different NOM or competing anions.

evidence_passages.passage: Batch tests used 100 mg/L PFOA or PFOS in laboratory pure water and groundwater to compare four strong-base AERs (HPA25M, PA312, UBA120) and one weak-base AER (WA30) plus a polymeric adsorbent (HP20).

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Results – Table 2, PFOA and PFOS adsorption kinetics (ResearchGate PDF p.5, Table 2)
evidence_passages.passage: Pseudo-second-order kinetic modeling gave equilibrium capacities q_e in pure water for PFOA of 931 mg/g (HPA25M), 1003 mg/g (PA312), 997 mg/g (UBA120) and 654 mg/g (WA30); PFOS q_e were 1007, 670, 244 and 548 mg/g, respectively.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Results – Table 2, groundwater vs pure water (ResearchGate PDF p.5, Table 2)
evidence_passages.passage: In groundwater, PFOA capacities dropped substantially (e.g., HPA25M q_e ≈348 mg/g vs 931 mg/g in pure water), whereas PFOS capacities on HPA25M remained high (~929 mg/g), indicating stronger selectivity for PFOS.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Results – SEM-EDX and pore structure (ResearchGate PDF p.6–7, Fig. 3–4)
evidence_passages.passage: SEM and pore-size analyses showed HPA25M had higher porosity and a substantial fraction of pores in the 1–10 nm range, which the authors link to more efficient and robust PFOS removal in groundwater.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Results – Spectroscopic characterization (ResearchGate PDF p.5–6, Fig. 3)
evidence_passages.passage: XPS/FTIR spectra indicated CF2-related peaks on resin surfaces after adsorption; PFOA and PFOS signals were strongest on HPA25M and PA312, supporting a mechanism combining electrostatic anion exchange with hydrophobic interactions in resin pores.

source_limitations: Batch experiments used very high initial PFAS concentrations (100 mg/L), above typical drinking water levels.
Only PFOA and PFOS were tested; short-chain PFAS and precursors were not evaluated.
Groundwater composition is site-specific and only partially characterized in the available text.
sources.title: Important properties of anion exchange resins for efficient removal of PFOS and PFOA from groundwater

sources.citation: Lesmeister L, Hale SE, Merklinger M, Horn H, Riegel M. The effect of inorganic anions on the adsorption of perfluoroalkyl acids to various polymeric anion exchange resins. Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering. 2024;12:114871.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Introduction/Methods – PFAAs and resins (PDF p.1–2, Table 1–2)
evidence_passages.passage: Eight PFAAs with 1–7 perfluorinated carbons (PFPrA, PFBA, PFPeA, PFHxA, PFOA, PFBS, PFHxS, PFOS) were tested on three polystyrenic AERs: A111 (weak-base tertiary amine), M600 (strong-base type II) and PSR2Plus (strong-base PFAS-selective).
Batch experiments varied NaCl and Na2SO4 concentrations between 0.5 and 3.8 mM to represent typical drinking water; resins were tested in their supplied ionic forms (A111 free base, others chloride).

Adsorption affinity increased with alkyl chain length and with longer alkyl moieties in the resin functional groups, following dimethylamines (A111) < dimethylethanolamines (M600) < tributylamines (PSR2Plus).

When both chloride and sulfate were present, sulfate caused stronger inhibition of PFAA adsorption on all resins; adsorption of short-chain PFCAs (C3–C4) was particularly sensitive to inorganic anion competition.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Methods/Results – modeling and breakthrough prediction (PDF p.1–2, lines 123–132)
evidence_passages.passage: For each resin and PFAA, the authors developed log–log relationships between residual aqueous PFAA concentration and inorganic anion concentration, then used these to estimate stoichiometric breakthrough bed volumes for fixed-bed filters under different water chemistries.

source_limitations: Experiments were batch rather than continuous-flow, so fixed-bed predictions rely on equilibrium-based modeling with acknowledged limitations.
NOM and more complex water matrices were not directly tested; focus is on inorganic anions in relatively clean solutions.
Ultra-short chain PFAS (e.g., TFA) and many precursors were not included.
sources.title: The effect of inorganic anions on the adsorption of perfluoroalkyl acids to various polymeric anion exchange resins

sources.citation: Hansen MC, Børresen MH, Schlabach M, Cornelissen G. Sorption of perfluorinated compounds from contaminated water to activated carbon. Journal of Soils and Sediments. 2010;10(2):179–185.

evidence_passages.passage: Batch sorption isotherms were measured for three perfluorosulfonates and five perfluoroacetic acids using contaminated groundwater from a PFAS-impacted well and both powdered and granular activated carbon.
For PFOS and PFOA, Freundlich coefficients log K_iF were about 4.0 and 3.8 for PAC and 2.7 and 2.3 for GAC, respectively, indicating stronger sorption to PAC at nanogram-per-liter levels.
Freundlich n values were generally around 0.5, and K_iF increased with PFAS chain length, with stronger chain-length dependence for sulfonates than carboxylates.
Short (10-minute) contact time tests still achieved 20–40% removal with GAC and 60–90% removal with PAC, suggesting adsorption kinetics fast enough for flow-through treatment.

source_limitations: Only abstract-level information was accessible; detailed conditions (exact PFAS identities, pH, DOC, AC doses) were not available.
Water matrix is a single contaminated groundwater; no comparison across matrices or added competitors.
PFAS precursors and many short-chain compounds were not covered.
sources.title: Sorption of perfluorinated compounds from contaminated water to activated carbon

sources.citation: Qian J, Shen M, Wang P, et al. Perfluorooctane sulfonate adsorption on powder activated carbon: Effect of phosphate (P) competition, pH, and temperature. Chemosphere. 2017;182:215–222.

evidence_passages.passage: Laboratory batch experiments with powdered activated carbon examined PFOS adsorption as a function of temperature, pH, and phosphate concentration in single-solute and binary PFOS–phosphate systems.
Higher temperature increased PFOS adsorption in both single and PFOS–phosphate systems; kinetic data were well described by pseudo second-order models.
Langmuir isotherms fitted PFOS adsorption well; enthalpy and entropy changes were positive while Gibbs free energy was negative, indicating spontaneous, endothermic adsorption.
In single-solute tests, PFOS adsorption decreased with increasing pH, consistent with reduced electrostatic attraction and changes in PFOS speciation at higher pH.

source_limitations: Full text with exact PFOS concentrations, PAC doses, and phosphate levels was not accessible.
Study considers only PFOS and phosphate as a competing anion; dissolved organic matter and other ions are not addressed.
Experiments are batch in simple solutions, not real groundwater or drinking water.
sources.title: Perfluorooctane sulfonate adsorption on powder activated carbon: Effect of phosphate (P) competition, pH, and temperature

sources.citation: Niarchos G, Georgii L, Ahrens L, Berggren Kleja D, Fagerlund F. A systematic study of the competitive sorption of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) on colloidal activated carbon. Ecotoxicology and Environmental Safety. 2023;264:115408.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Methods – CAC and soil properties (PDF p.2, lines 193–203, 223–229)
evidence_passages.passage: Colloidal activated carbon (PlumeStop, 20% AC, ~900 m²/g, 1–2 µm particles, zeta potential −80 to −2 mV at pH 7) was mixed with a low-organic soil (0.6% organic carbon) at 0.2% w/w (0.004 g CAC per 2 g soil).

Seven PFAS (PFPeA, PFHpA, PFNA, PFBS, PFHxS, PFOS and FOSA) were tested as single solutes, binary pairs and a seven-compound mixture over 0.002–0.05 mmol/L, in 40 mL aqueous solution (Milli-Q water with 1 mM CaCl2) at L/S = 20 and 14-day equilibration.
Average PFAS removal in single-solute systems was 77%±7.8%, versus 67%±7.1% in the multi-solute mixture, showing a roughly 10% drop in treatment effectiveness due to competition.

Single-solute removal ranged from about 99.8% (FOSA at 0.002 mmol/L) to 41% (PFOS at 0.05 mmol/L), while in the mixture removal ranged from 99.8% (FOSA at 0.0003 mmol/L) to 44% (PFOS at 0.007 mmol/L).

Distribution coefficients Kd were generally higher for longer-chain PFAS and FOSA; sorption was often non-linear, indicating concentration-dependent competition effects that varied with PFAS structure.

source_limitations: Experiments are soil–CAC slurry batch tests rather than pure water or engineered filter beds; water matrix contains added CaCl2 but little DOC.
Only seven PFAS were investigated; key short-chain PFCAs below C4 and several emerging PFAS are excluded.
The study does not include direct cost or energy data, though CAC dose (0.2% w/w) is specified.
sources.title: A systematic study of the competitive sorption of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) on colloidal activated carbon

sources.citation: Bano A, Prasad B, Dave H, Prasad KS. Efficient adsorption of perfluorooctane sulfonate and perfluorobutane sulfonic acid from aqueous solution onto amine-functionalized diatomite granules. Scientific Reports. 2026;16:10368.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Introduction/Methods – Adsorbent and target PFAS (HTML p.1–2, lines 42–45, 80–83)
evidence_passages.passage: Granules of diatomaceous earth functionalized with (3-aminopropyl)triethoxysilane (APTES-DE) were synthesized and tested in fixed-bed configuration for adsorption of PFOS (long-chain PFSA) and PFBS (short-chain PFSA) from aqueous solution.

Maximum removal efficiencies reached about 92.4% for PFOS and 89.9% for PFBS under optimized conditions, with Freundlich isotherms providing the best fit and indicating multilayer adsorption on heterogeneous surfaces.
Regeneration tests over five sorption–desorption cycles showed only modest losses in capacity, with adsorption performance decreasing by roughly 4.6% for PFOS and 3.6% for PFBS after the fifth cycle.

The authors attribute high performance of APTES-DE to positively charged amine groups providing strong electrostatic interactions with anionic PFAS, supplemented by hydrophobic interactions for longer-chain PFOS.

source_limitations: Full numerical isotherm parameters, flow rates, and influent PFAS concentrations are not fully captured here.
Study uses synthetic solutions; effects of NOM, competing inorganic ions, and complex wastewaters are only discussed qualitatively.
Focus is limited to two PFSAs (PFOS, PFBS); PFCAs and precursors are not tested.
sources.title: Efficient adsorption of perfluorooctane sulfonate and perfluorobutane sulfonic acid from aqueous solution onto amine-functionalized diatomite granules
